name: Human rights
scope: Human rights as the Stanford and Internet Encyclopedias of Philosophy, Britannica and the UN's own accounts define them: moral rights held by every person simply as a human being, protected by national and international law, and codified since 1948 in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the two 1966 covenants (the International Bill of Human Rights), with their philosophical grounding in natural-rights theory (Locke) and Kantian dignity and agency (Kant, Gewirth, Shue, Griffin). It covers the doctrine that individuals hold universal civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights, and the international system built on it. It excludes the work of particular NGOs, parties or governments that invoke human rights, other ideologies' own rights doctrines (liberalism, socialism) except where these sources tie them to human rights, and critics of human rights.

summary: Human rights is the doctrine that every person holds basic rights simply as a human being, regardless of citizenship, birth, sex, race or religion, and that states must protect them under law. Its core texts, the Universal Declaration and the two 1966 covenants, cover civil and political rights (life, freedom from torture, fair trial, expression, religion, political participation) and economic, social and cultural rights (work, fair pay, health, education, an adequate standard of living). It treats the rights as universal, inalienable and indivisible, and also protects the self-determination of peoples. Philosophers justify them through natural rights, human dignity and agency.
